Respiratory Virus Outbreak Disrupts Technology Hardware Production in Chile

SANTIAGO, June 18—A surge of acute respiratory virus cases among workers in Chile’s technology hardware industry has led to significant disruptions at several production sites across the country, industry representatives confirmed Tuesday. The outbreak, first detected late last week at two assembly plants in the Santiago Metropolitan Region, has rapidly spread to facilities in Valparaíso and the Biobío region, prompting partial shutdowns and reduced operational capacity.

The Chilean Association of Technology Hardware Manufacturers (CATHM) reported that more than 340 workers have tested positive for the virus, identified by health authorities as a variant of human metapneumovirus (hMPV). In response, firms have implemented emergency protocols including on-site testing, enhanced sanitation, and staggered shifts. “Our primary concern is the health and safety of our workforce,” said CATHM spokesperson Camila Herrera. “We are coordinating closely with local health officials and have suspended non-essential operations at some affected plants.”

Among the hardest hit is Sicolsa Technologies, which operates a major circuit board assembly facility in San Bernardo. The company disclosed that nearly 18% of its 1,200-strong staff are currently on sick leave. “We’re running our lines at about half of normal capacity,” said Sicolsa’s operations manager, Felipe Rojas. “Delays are inevitable, but we are working to maintain critical deliveries where possible.”

Similar disruptions have been reported at Microtrol, a manufacturer of industrial sensors, and Datamarx, known for its consumer electronics components. Both firms have confirmed temporary closures of select production lines and a shift to remote work for eligible employees. According to a statement from Datamarx, “Efforts are underway to minimize the impact on output, but the situation remains highly fluid.”

Trade unions representing technology hardware workers have called for greater support and additional paid sick leave. “Many workers are anxious about their health and job security,” said Paula Contreras, president of the National Union of Technology Hardware Workers. “We urge employers to prioritize people over output during this challenging time.”

Industry analysts estimate the outbreak could reduce overall production output by 20% to 35% this month if current trends persist. “The Chilean technology hardware sector, known for its growing role in regional supply chains, is facing its most serious labor shortage in over a decade,” said analyst Rodrigo Vidal of Capital Andino Consultores.

Authorities and industry leaders are monitoring the situation, with further updates expected as the outbreak develops. At present, no timeline has been set for a return to normal operations.
